ApexTrace: driving signatures from low-rate public Formula 1 telemetry

Sadman Zaman · CSE undergraduate, BUET · November 2026 · code, data and full report: github.com/SadMan-ZaMaN/ApexTrace

The question

Formula 1's public timing feed gives each car's speed, throttle, gear, an on/off brake flag and position only about 3.77 times per second, on a 40 ms clock with gaps, so nothing faster than 1.89 Hz can be resolved. Can signal processing still measure where and how a driver brakes and accelerates through each corner, precisely enough to tell two teammates apart on weekends a model has never seen? And how much of such a "signature" belongs to the driver rather than the car?

Approach

  • Measure the instrument first. Synthetic laps with a known truth (realistic speed profiles, the feed's irregular sampling and dropouts) give the error of every estimator by Monte Carlo. The obvious brake point, the first brake-on sample, is 12.5 m late on average; a speed breakpoint inside the off→on interval has 4.2 m error. A causal 5-sample moving average shifts a braking event by 25.1 m (group delay), so events are located on the raw samples and never after smoothing.
  • One track coordinate. Integrated speed is smooth but drifts; projected position does not drift but is noisy. A simple complementary filter combines them in each corner window (random error about 1.15 m).
  • Features. 11 per driver, lap and corner (brake onset, minimum speed, throttle pickup, …), relative to the field.
  • Honest tests. Identification is always tested on whole weekends held out of training, against lap time, whole-lap statistics and shuffled labels. The 2025 and 2026 seasons were locked in the code and tested once, after their test plans had been committed (preregistration).

Data: qualifying 2023–2024 for development (46 sessions, 4,500 kept laps, 21,493 clean corner passes); 2025 (23 sessions) and 2026 up to a fixed cutoff (19 sessions) as held-out seasons.

Results

QuestionResultVerdict
H1Are corner features repeatable? ICC per lap 0.15–0.58 (2 of 30 at 0.5 or more); per weekend 0.04–0.40 weak to moderate
H2Do two teammates differ beyond the measurement error? (pilot) 0 of 27 comparisons after correction, with 2–4 laps each not shown (as predicted)
H3Do the features tell teammates apart on unseen weekends? 2025: balanced accuracy 0.662 vs 0.575 for lap time, 8 of 10 teams, p = 0.027; whole-lap statistics 0.680 supported, replicated
H4Does the signature follow drivers who change teams? 2025: 2 of 5 changers closer to their own past than to the new teammate, p = 0.81 not supported
H5Does it survive the 2026 change of technical rules? 13 of 19 drivers closer to their own 2025 signature, p = 0.084 (14 needed; without a rule change 16 of 20 and 14 of 16) not supported

Balanced accuracy: 0.5 = guessing. ICC: the share of variation between drivers. H4, H5: one-sided sign tests over drivers.

What it means

  • Corner-level measurements with known errors separate teammates on unseen weekends, and the result held on a season kept back until the end. What they separate is the driver together with their side of the garage (set-up, parts, qualifying segment reached); simple whole-lap statistics do as well, and the corner features' value is that they show where two drivers differ.
  • Neither a change of team nor the 2026 rule change showed the signature following the driver. With 19 drivers (treated as independent) the 2026 test had only 47 % power against a true share of 0.7, so a weakened signature cannot be ruled out.
  • The feed sets hard limits: the usable share of corner passes fell from 0.84 (2024) to 0.61 (2026), and every claim is limited to what about 3.77 samples per second can show.

Next steps I would like to work on

Teammate-relative features, in which the shared car cancels like common-mode noise in a differential amplifier (an exploratory check already points that way); a learned model on the raw corner traces under the same held-out protocol (the design is written down); and 2027 as the next untouched season, to tell a weakened signature from a lost one.

Built in October–November 2026 as my first research project. The code and much of the text were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude) under my direction; I set the questions and the plan and reviewed every change. Every number in this summary and in the report is generated from the result files and checked by automated tests. ApexTrace is unofficial and not associated with Formula 1; the timing data were read through the free OpenF1 and FastF1 interfaces.
